---
title: "Risk-adjustment models"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dpi = 96)
```

The risk-adjustment model is where the provider effects come from. This
page explains the choices the package offers (fixed, random or correlated
random provider effects; logistic, linear or Cox models; the Firth
penalty) and when each is the right one. Every fitter takes a `pp_data()`
object and returns a fit that `summary()`, `standardize()`, `test()`,
`confint()` and `plot()` understand.

## Provider effects as fixed effects

The model is $\eta_{ijk} = \gamma_i + Z_{ijk}^\top\beta$ with one free
parameter $\gamma_i$ per provider. Two things follow.

**The effects are never shrunk.** A random-effect model pulls every
provider toward the average, by more for small providers; a fixed-effect
model reports what the data say about each provider and lets the test
express how uncertain that is. For a measure that reports the provider,
the fixed-effect estimate is the estimand.

**The pooled model is biased.** Dropping the provider effects and fitting
$Z^\top\beta$ alone estimates not $\beta$ but, in the linear case,
$\beta + \rho\,\sigma_\gamma / \sigma_Z$ when a risk factor is correlated
at $\rho$ with the provider effect: a bias that does not vanish with the
sample size. Case mix is related to the provider (geography, referral
patterns, the patients' circumstances), so $\rho \ne 0$ is the normal
state of affairs. For binary outcomes the bias need not vanish even at
$\rho = 0$, because of the non-collapsibility of the logit link.

With thousands of providers the fixed-effect model has thousands of
parameters, which general-purpose software handles by expanding every
provider into an indicator column. The package does not: the block of the
information matrix that belongs to the provider effects is diagonal, so
each effect is updated from its own provider's records (the serial
block-wise inversion Newton algorithm, SerBIN, of Wu et al. 2022), and a
fit with ten thousand providers takes seconds.

## Binary and binomial outcomes: `fit_logistic_fe()`

```{r}
library(pprof)
d <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 60, provider_size = c(15, 60), seed = 7)
pd <- pp_data(d, y = "y", x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider",
              patient = "patient", message = FALSE)
fit <- fit_logistic_fe(pd)
fit
str(coef(fit))
```

* `algorithm = "SerBIN"` (default) or `"BAN"` (block ascent Newton, the
  older alternating algorithm; slower, kept for reference).
* `bound`: provider effects are kept within `median(gamma) ± bound` on
  the logit scale (default 10), which is where providers with no events or
  with all events end up.
* A binomial outcome (events out of `n` trials per row, for instance
  hospital days out of days at risk in a month) uses the same fitter once
  `pp_data()` was given `n`; every later step accounts for the trials.

The risk-factor coefficients with their tests:

```{r}
summary(fit)
summary(fit, test = "robust_wald")
```

`summary()` offers the model-based Wald test, the patient-clustered robust
Wald test, the likelihood-ratio test (a refit without the covariate) and
the score test. The variance of the provider effects is `vcov(fit)`'s
attribute `var_gamma`, and `gamma_variance()` returns the variance the
Wald test uses (`"case_mix"`, the variance of the provider's fitted
average linear predictor, or `"full"`, the variance of $\hat\gamma_i$
alone; see [Tests of provider effects](testing.html)).

### Providers whose outcomes are all the same: the Firth penalty

A provider with no events has no finite maximum-likelihood effect (it sits
at the lower bound). The Firth penalty, half the log determinant of the
information, gives every provider a finite estimate and reduces the
small-sample bias of the others (Firth 1993). The fit is a `logistic_fe`
object like any other, so every test applies; the likelihood-ratio tests
compare penalized likelihoods.

```{r}
firth <- fit_logistic_fe(pd, penalty = "firth")
range(coef(fit)$gamma)
range(coef(firth)$gamma)
```

The kernel follows ParaFLR (Shao and He): provider-level work on
independent threads (`threads`), with the reductions arranged so that the
result does not depend on the thread count.

## Continuous outcomes: `fit_linear_fe()`

A continuous outcome (a laboratory value, a length of stay) uses the linear
fixed-effect model, fitted as a within-provider regression (every variable
centred by provider), which never forms the provider indicators either.

```{r}
dc <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 40, type = "continuous", seed = 8)
pc <- pp_data(dc, y = "y", x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider",
              patient = "patient", message = FALSE)
lin <- fit_linear_fe(pc)
lin
summary(lin)
```

The model-based tests of a linear fit use the $t$ distribution with
$n - m - p$ degrees of freedom; the standardized measures are differences
rather than ratios.

## Random and correlated random effects

For comparison with the fixed-effect fit, and for the settings where a
shrunken estimate is wanted, the package wraps lme4:

* `fit_logistic_re()`, `fit_linear_re()`: a random provider intercept,
  $\gamma_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$; the reported effects are the predicted
  (shrunken) values, `coefficients$alpha`, with conditional variances
  `post_var`.
* `fit_logistic_cre()`, `fit_linear_cre()`: correlated random effects
  (Mundlak), which add every risk factor's provider mean to the fixed part
  (`<x>_between`) next to its within-provider deviation (`<x>_within`), so
  that the random effect is no longer assumed independent of the case mix.
  The within coefficients equal the fixed-effect coefficients in the linear
  case.

```{r}
re <- fit_logistic_re(pd)
re
cre <- fit_logistic_cre(pd)
summary(cre)
```

`standardize()` of a random-effect fit offers `numerator = "observed"` or
`"predicted"` (the predicted-to-expected ratio), and `test()` is the Wald
test of the predicted effect.

## Time-to-event outcomes: `fit_cox()`

For a survival outcome (death, a first admission) or recurrent events
counted on patient-records (admissions, transfusions) the model is a
proportional-hazards model, and the provider effect is handled by
**stratification**: each provider has its own baseline hazard, which
absorbs its effect, and the risk-factor coefficients are estimated within
providers. The national baseline is then the Breslow estimator over every
record with the fitted linear predictor as an offset (the two-stage model
of He and Schaubel 2014). The expected number of events of every record is
$E = e^{\eta} [\Lambda_0(\text{stop}) - \Lambda_0(\text{start})]$, and
the provider's measure is its observed-to-expected ratio.

```{r}
s <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 60, provider_size = c(15, 60), type = "survival", seed = 9)
ps <- pp_data(s, x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider", patient = "patient",
              time = "stop", start = "start", event = "event", cutoff = 0, message = FALSE)
cox <- fit_cox(ps)
cox
summary(cox, variance = "robust")
head(standardize(cox))
```

* `strata = "provider"` (default) or `"none"` for the pooled baseline.
* `x2`: covariates fitted in a second stage with the first-stage linear
  predictor as offset (calendar-year indicators, say).
* `ties = "breslow"` (default) or `"efron"`.
* Case `weights` and an `offset` declared in `pp_data()` are used
  (recurrent-event measures weight each record by its number of events and
  carry a log-exposure offset).
* The patient column is the cluster of the robust covariance.
* `cutoff = 0`: every provider enters the stratified fit; the providers to
  report are chosen by `test(cox, min_expected = 3)`.

The discrete-time hazard model (one logistic hazard per period, with
provider effects) is fitted by `var_select(ps, model = "discrete")`, see
[Variable selection](selection.html).

## Which model

| Outcome | Fitter | The provider effect is | Measure |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0/1 per row, or events out of trials | `fit_logistic_fe()` | a log-odds | ratio or rate |
| continuous | `fit_linear_fe()` | a difference of means | difference |
| time to event, recurrent events | `fit_cox()` | absorbed in the provider's baseline | observed / expected |
| any, when a shrunken estimate is wanted | `fit_*_re()`, `fit_*_cre()` | a predicted random effect | ratio, rate or difference |

rates in dialysis facilities; adjusting for hospital effects. *Lifetime

inference for profiling health care providers. *Statistics in Medicine*,
41(15), 2840-2853.

*Biometrika*, 80(1), 27-38.

He K, Schaubel DE (2014). Standardized mortality ratio for evaluating
center-specific mortality: assessment and alternative. *Statistics in
Biosciences*, 6(2), 1-19.
